rationales.A: Incorrect. ElastiCache is an in-memory cache and does not provide serverless SQL over S3 files.
rationales.B: Incorrect. A provisioned relational database adds administration and unnecessary ingestion for occasional lake queries.
rationales.C: Correct. Athena is serverless SQL over data in S3 and avoids provisioning a persistent database cluster.
rationales.D: Incorrect. SNS routes notifications and is not an analytical SQL query engine.

questions.central_requirement: Identify the serverless query service for SQL directly over S3 data.
questions.decisive_words: occasional SQL, Parquet, S3, no cluster
questions.reusable_rule: Use Athena for ad hoc serverless SQL over S3; optimize cost with columnar formats, compression, and useful partition pruning.

questions.stem: A data lake receives daily CSV exports and continuous JSON events. The company needs managed transformation into partitioned Parquet, a shared catalog for Athena, and fine-grained cross-account table permissions. Which three components meet the requirements?

options.A: Use AWS Glue jobs or appropriate Glue serverless ETL capabilities to transform source data into Parquet.
options.B: Use AWS Glue Data Catalog for table schemas and partition metadata.
options.C: Use AWS Lake Formation to govern supported table, column, and cross-account data permissions.
options.D: Use Amazon Route 53 hosted zones as the schema registry.
options.E: Use EBS snapshots as the cross-account permission system for S3 tables.
options.F: Use Amazon Polly to convert JSON events into Parquet files.

rationales.A: Correct. Glue provides managed data integration and Spark-based transformation without self-managing a cluster.
rationales.B: Correct. The shared catalog stores technical metadata that Athena and other analytics services can use.
rationales.C: Correct. Lake Formation centralizes fine-grained data-lake permissions on cataloged resources.
rationales.D: Incorrect. DNS records do not store analytical schemas or partition metadata.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Block-storage snapshots neither govern S3 tables nor provide column-level permissions.
rationales.F: Incorrect. Polly performs text-to-speech and is unrelated to data format transformation.

questions.central_requirement: Transform heterogeneous inputs, catalog the lake, and govern fine-grained cross-account access.
questions.decisive_words: CSV and JSON, Parquet, shared catalog, fine-grained permissions
questions.reusable_rule: A governed lake separates transformation, metadata catalog, and authorization into Glue processing, Glue Data Catalog, and Lake Formation.

questions.stem: A compliance archive ingests objects into S3 Standard, reads most during the first month, rarely reads them for six years, and must delete them after year seven. Retrieval after month one can take hours. Which design minimizes storage cost while preserving automated retention?

options.A: Move objects to S3 One Zone-IA even if the archive requires resilience to loss of an Availability Zone.
options.B: Keep every object in S3 Standard for seven years because lifecycle transitions always reduce durability.
options.C: Copy every object to EC2 instance store after one month.
options.D: Use an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition eligible objects to an appropriate Glacier class after the active period and expire them after the required retention boundary.

rationales.A: Incorrect. One Zone-IA stores data in one AZ and is inappropriate when the archive cannot be recreated after a zonal loss.
rationales.B: Incorrect. S3 storage classes are designed for different access patterns and retain documented durability; Standard wastes cost for cold data.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Instance store is ephemeral, host-bound, and unsuitable for a seven-year compliance archive.
rationales.D: Correct. Lifecycle automation aligns storage class with access age and performs expiration without manual object-by-object operations.

questions.central_requirement: Align automatic storage transitions and expiration with a known access and retention timeline.
questions.decisive_words: first month active, six years rare, hours acceptable, delete year seven
questions.reusable_rule: When object age predicts access, use S3 Lifecycle transitions and expiration; validate minimum storage duration and retrieval requirements.

questions.stem: A database uses a 2 TiB gp2 EBS volume only to obtain sufficient baseline IOPS, but actual capacity needs are 500 GiB. Performance monitoring shows 6,000 IOPS and 250 MiB/s are adequate. Which change is most cost-effective?

options.A: Migrate to a properly sized gp3 volume and provision the required IOPS and throughput independently of capacity.
options.B: Increase the gp2 volume to 4 TiB so baseline IOPS doubles.
options.C: Move the database files to EC2 instance store without replication.
options.D: Create hourly EBS snapshots and use snapshots as the live database volume.

rationales.A: Correct. gp3 decouples performance settings from volume size, allowing lower capacity while meeting measured IOPS and throughput.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Increasing unused capacity raises cost and ignores a volume type that decouples performance from size.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Instance store is ephemeral and would endanger database durability after stop, termination, or host failure.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Snapshots are point-in-time backups and cannot directly serve as the attached live filesystem.

questions.central_requirement: Reduce EBS overprovisioning while retaining measured IOPS and throughput.
questions.decisive_words: gp2 sized for IOPS, unused capacity, 6000 IOPS, 250 MiB/s
questions.reusable_rule: Use gp3 when independent capacity, IOPS, and throughput sizing avoids paying for unused gp2 storage.

questions.stem: A document repository has unpredictable object access: some files are opened weekly, others become cold for months, and access patterns change without notice. The team wants automatic savings without retrieval fees or operational analysis of each object. Which class is best?

options.A: Put every object immediately into S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
options.B: Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering and enable the archive tiers only if their retrieval behavior is acceptable.
options.C: Keep all objects permanently in S3 Standard, manually review every access log each day, and change storage classes by hand.
options.D: Store the repository on one EC2 instance store volume.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Deep Archive has long retrieval times and minimum-duration considerations that conflict with unpredictable weekly reads.
rationales.B: Correct. Intelligent-Tiering moves objects among access tiers based on observed activity without retrieval fees for the automatic frequent and infrequent tiers.
rationales.C: Incorrect. This preserves performance but fails the automatic savings and low-operations requirements.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Instance store is ephemeral and is not durable managed object storage.

questions.central_requirement: Optimize unpredictable S3 access automatically without per-object analysis.
questions.decisive_words: unpredictable access, changes, automatic savings, no retrieval fees
questions.reusable_rule: Use Intelligent-Tiering when access patterns are unknown or changing; evaluate monitoring charges, object size, and optional archive retrieval times.

questions.stem: A storage review must distinguish durable block, shared file, and archival object options before optimization. Which three statements are correct?

options.A: Amazon EBS volumes provide persistent block storage for supported EC2 attachment patterns within an Availability Zone.
options.B: EC2 instance store is the preferred durable system of record after an instance is stopped or terminated.
options.C: A NAT Gateway is a shared POSIX file system for private subnets.
options.D: Amazon EFS provides managed shared file access for multiple Linux clients across Availability Zones in a Region.
options.E: S3 Glacier storage classes are object-storage archival tiers with retrieval-time and minimum-duration tradeoffs.
options.F: CloudFront edge caches are authoritative block-device backups for EBS volumes.

rationales.A: Correct. EBS is durable block storage scoped to an Availability Zone and supports snapshots for backup or migration.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Instance store data is ephemeral and can be lost on stop, termination, or host failure.
rationales.C: Incorrect. NAT Gateways translate network egress and do not expose file-system semantics.
rationales.D: Correct. EFS is a regional managed NFS file service designed for concurrent client access.
rationales.E: Correct. Glacier classes reduce storage cost for cold objects while introducing retrieval and duration considerations.
rationales.F: Incorrect. CloudFront caches delivered content and is not an EBS backup or block-storage service.

questions.central_requirement: Recognize the storage model and durability role of EBS, EFS, and S3 archival classes.
questions.decisive_words: block, shared file, archival object, optimization
questions.reusable_rule: Choose storage by access protocol, scope, durability, and retrieval profile before comparing price; caches and ephemeral disks are not backups.

questions.stem: A company runs steady EC2 and Fargate production workloads in several Regions, but instance families may change during modernization. It can commit to a consistent hourly compute spend for three years. Which discount model offers the most flexibility?

options.A: Use Spot Instances for every production task regardless of interruption tolerance.
options.B: Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for one exact family and assume they cover Fargate.
options.C: Purchase a Compute Savings Plan sized to the conservative baseline spend.
options.D: Prepay three years of NAT Gateway hourly charges as a Savings Plan.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Spot discounts require interruption-tolerant workloads and do not represent a guaranteed baseline commitment.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Standard RIs are less flexible and do not provide the requested cross-service Fargate coverage.
rationales.C: Correct. Compute Savings Plans apply across eligible EC2 families, Regions, operating systems, and supported Fargate or Lambda usage.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Savings Plans apply to eligible compute usage, not NAT Gateway charges.

questions.central_requirement: Discount a stable compute baseline while retaining family, Region, and service flexibility.
questions.decisive_words: steady EC2 and Fargate, families may change, three-year commitment
questions.reusable_rule: Buy flexible commitments only for a conservative usage baseline; keep variable or interruption-tolerant demand on appropriate on-demand or Spot capacity.

questions.stem: A rendering platform has a steady queue plus large overnight bursts. Jobs checkpoint every five minutes and can be retried on interruption. The company wants guaranteed baseline completion capacity and the lowest cost for burst capacity. Which design is best?

options.A: Move the render queue to Glacier Deep Archive and retrieve it before each job.
options.B: Run every worker on one Spot instance type in one Availability Zone with no interruption handling.
options.C: Reserve peak On-Demand capacity all day even though bursts occur only overnight.
options.D: Run the baseline on On-Demand or committed compute and scale the retryable burst workers on EC2 Spot capacity diversified across instance types and Availability Zones.

rationales.A: Incorrect. An archival object tier is not a compute-capacity or queue-scaling mechanism.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Single-pool Spot capacity is fragile, and lack of checkpoint or interruption response wastes work.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Permanent peak capacity meets performance but wastes substantial idle compute cost.
rationales.D: Correct. Stable capacity protects deadlines while diversified Spot handles interruption-tolerant bursts at lower cost.

questions.central_requirement: Blend reliable baseline compute with discounted interruption-tolerant burst capacity.
questions.decisive_words: steady queue, overnight bursts, checkpoint, retry, lowest cost
questions.reusable_rule: Use stable capacity for the noninterruptible baseline and diversified Spot for elastic fault-tolerant work, with checkpointing and rebalance handling.

questions.stem: A Lambda image transformation function uses 512 MB and runs for 12 seconds. Testing shows that 1,536 MB finishes in 3 seconds, and both configurations meet correctness requirements. What should the team do before choosing the cheaper setting?

options.A: Compare measured GB-seconds, request charges, and downstream effects for both configurations, then select the best cost-performance point.
options.B: Always select the minimum memory because Lambda price depends only on configured memory.
options.C: Always select maximum memory because shorter execution is automatically free.
options.D: Move the function to a public subnet because public subnets reduce Lambda GB-second pricing.

rationales.A: Correct. Lambda allocates CPU with memory and bills duration, so higher memory can reduce total cost when execution time falls enough.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Billing depends on both memory and duration, and more memory also changes available CPU performance.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Higher memory has a higher per-duration rate and must be evaluated against the measured speedup.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Subnet selection does not change the Lambda compute billing formula and does not automatically provide a public IP.

questions.central_requirement: Optimize Lambda memory and duration using measured total cost rather than one dimension.
questions.decisive_words: 512 MB 12 seconds, 1536 MB 3 seconds, cost-performance
questions.reusable_rule: Benchmark representative Lambda memory sizes because CPU scales with memory and the cheapest configuration depends on memory-duration product and workload behavior.

questions.stem: A database estate includes predictable production RDS instances, an Aurora cluster with high I/O charges, and development databases idle every night. Which three actions should be evaluated for cost optimization without violating workload requirements?

options.A: Delete automated backups for production because recovery does not affect cost architecture.
options.B: Purchase appropriate Reserved DB Instances for the stable, well-measured RDS baseline.
options.C: Scale every database to the largest instance class to reduce query duration.
options.D: Compare Aurora I/O-Optimized with the standard configuration using the cluster's actual I/O-to-compute cost profile.
options.E: Convert relational workloads with joins and constraints to ElastiCache without application analysis.
options.F: Schedule supported nonproduction DB instances to stop and start during verified idle windows.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Removing required recovery points violates resilience and may create unacceptable business risk.
rationales.B: Correct. Reserved DB Instance pricing can discount eligible steady database instance usage when the commitment matches the workload.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Oversizing raises cost and may not improve bottlenecks unrelated to CPU or memory.
rationales.D: Correct. I/O-Optimized can reduce total cost for I/O-intensive Aurora workloads but is not automatically cheaper for every cluster.
rationales.E: Incorrect. A cache is not a durable relational system of record and cannot replace required SQL semantics.
rationales.F: Correct. Stopping eligible development databases avoids instance charges during planned idle periods while storage charges continue.

questions.central_requirement: Reduce database cost through commitments, pricing-model analysis, and idle-environment scheduling.
questions.decisive_words: predictable RDS, Aurora I/O charges, development idle
questions.reusable_rule: Optimize database cost only after separating steady commitments, measured I/O economics, idle schedules, and mandatory resilience requirements.

questions.stem: A new DynamoDB application has unknown and highly variable request traffic. The team wants to avoid capacity forecasting and throttling caused by an incorrect initial provisioned setting. Which capacity mode is the simplest starting choice?

options.A: Use provisioned capacity fixed permanently at one read and one write unit.
options.B: Use DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode.
options.C: Use an EC2 Auto Scaling group to add DynamoDB partitions manually.
options.D: Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering as the table capacity controller.

rationales.A: Incorrect. A tiny fixed allocation risks throttling and directly conflicts with unknown variable demand.
rationales.B: Correct. On-demand automatically accommodates variable traffic within service behavior and charges per request without initial capacity planning.
rationales.C: Incorrect. DynamoDB is managed and does not expose partitions as EC2 instances for customers to scale.
rationales.D: Incorrect. S3 storage tiers do not control DynamoDB request capacity.

questions.central_requirement: Choose a DynamoDB mode that removes initial capacity forecasting for variable demand.
questions.decisive_words: new application, unknown variable traffic, avoid forecasting
questions.reusable_rule: Start unpredictable DynamoDB workloads on on-demand capacity, then evaluate provisioned plus auto scaling when traffic becomes stable and savings justify it.

questions.stem: An Aurora workload's monthly I/O charges consistently exceed its instance charges, and load testing confirms the same high read and write volume after query tuning. The team wants predictable database cost without reducing throughput. What should it evaluate?

options.A: Move all tables to one Lambda execution environment's temporary storage and rely on environment reuse to persist the database between invocations.
options.B: Disable database backups and transaction logging to remove I/O.
options.C: Compare the cluster's measured break-even point with Aurora I/O-Optimized and switch if the total cost is lower.
options.D: Add more cross-Region replicas solely to reduce primary I/O billing.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Lambda temporary storage is ephemeral, not shared, and cannot replace a transactional database.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Disabling recovery protections violates durability and is not an appropriate cost optimization.
rationales.C: Correct. I/O-Optimized removes per-I/O charges in exchange for different compute and storage pricing, benefiting sufficiently I/O-intensive workloads.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Additional replicas add cost and replication I/O and do not automatically reduce the workload's write volume.

questions.central_requirement: Evaluate Aurora pricing configuration from the workload's measured I/O cost profile.
questions.decisive_words: I/O charges exceed instances, tuned workload, preserve throughput
questions.reusable_rule: Compare Aurora Standard and I/O-Optimized with real compute, storage, and I/O usage; choose by total cost, not one line item.

questions.stem: A global download service sends large immutable objects from an S3 origin to users on five continents. Costs are dominated by repeated origin transfer, NAT processing from private application hosts, and cross-AZ calls to a centralized NAT Gateway. Which redesign best improves both cost and resilience?

options.A: Copy the objects to EBS volumes attached to a single web server.
options.B: Assign public IPv4 addresses to every private host and bypass all security controls.
options.C: Route all Regions through one NAT Gateway in the origin Region.
options.D: Serve cacheable objects through CloudFront, use an S3 gateway endpoint for private host access, and route remaining egress through zonally aligned NAT Gateways where volume and resilience justify them.

rationales.A: Incorrect. A single block-storage origin is operationally fragile and cannot match global object caching.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Public exposure is not a safe cost optimization and creates ongoing IPv4 charges.
rationales.C: Incorrect. NAT Gateways are regional resources, and cross-Region centralization would add latency, transfer cost, and failure risk.
rationales.D: Correct. Caching reduces repeated origin delivery, the endpoint removes S3 from NAT, and same-AZ NAT paths avoid cross-AZ dependency and transfer.

questions.central_requirement: Reduce repeated content delivery, NAT processing, and cross-AZ egress dependency together.
questions.decisive_words: global downloads, repeated origin, S3 through NAT, centralized NAT
questions.reusable_rule: Optimize network cost by changing traffic paths: edge caching for repeated content, service endpoints for AWS APIs, and zonally resilient egress for the remainder.

questions.stem: A multi-AZ application transfers terabytes each month to S3, sends static responses globally, and uses interface endpoints for services that support gateway endpoints. Which three actions directly target recurring network charges?

options.A: Send S3 traffic through a NAT Gateway in a different Availability Zone.
options.B: Disable compression for all text responses.
options.C: Use an S3 gateway endpoint for VPC-to-S3 traffic and associate the required route tables.
options.D: Add public IPv4 addresses to all instances solely to avoid endpoint hourly charges.
options.E: Cache eligible static content with CloudFront and tune cache keys and TTLs.
options.F: Review endpoint type and consolidate or remove unnecessary interface endpoints while preserving required private connectivity.

rationales.A: Incorrect. This retains NAT processing and adds cross-AZ transfer and a zonal dependency.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Larger payloads generally increase transfer rather than reduce it.
rationales.C: Correct. S3 gateway endpoints avoid NAT processing and have no additional endpoint hourly charge.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Public addresses add cost and exposure and do not provide an appropriate private service path.
rationales.E: Correct. A higher cache-hit ratio reduces repeated origin requests and data transfer from the origin path.
rationales.F: Correct. Interface endpoints incur hourly and data-processing charges, so architecture and AZ placement should match actual needs.

questions.central_requirement: Reduce recurring service-path, origin-delivery, and unnecessary endpoint charges.
questions.decisive_words: terabytes to S3, static global, interface versus gateway endpoints
questions.reusable_rule: Network cost optimization starts with flow visibility, then replaces expensive paths with gateway endpoints, caching, compression, or right-sized private endpoints.

questions.stem: A company exports 8 TB of analytics data from AWS to the same on-premises facility every month. The transfer is steady, internet performance is inconsistent, and finance wants a predictable private connectivity model. Which option should be evaluated first?

options.A: Evaluate AWS Direct Connect capacity and data-transfer pricing against the steady volume and required redundancy.
options.B: Create a larger NAT Gateway because NAT provides a dedicated circuit to the facility, and assign it a fixed public IP for deterministic routing.
options.C: Use an S3 gateway endpoint from the on-premises network through Transit Gateway.
options.D: Send the monthly dataset through Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints.

rationales.A: Correct. Direct Connect can provide more consistent private connectivity and different transfer economics for sustained hybrid traffic.
rationales.B: Incorrect. A NAT Gateway is internet egress translation and does not create a private dedicated on-premises circuit.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Gateway endpoints cannot be extended from on-premises through VPN, Direct Connect, peering, or Transit Gateway.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Resolver endpoints forward DNS queries, not bulk analytics data.

questions.central_requirement: Evaluate predictable private hybrid connectivity for sustained outbound data volume.
questions.decisive_words: 8 TB monthly, same facility, inconsistent internet, predictable private
questions.reusable_rule: For steady high-volume hybrid transfer, compare Direct Connect port, provider, redundancy, and data-transfer economics with internet or VPN alternatives.
